ActivationFunctions

The per-neuron function that runs after the weighted sum — and the reason “deep learning” is allowed to be deep.

STEP · SIGMOID · TANH · RELU + THE MSE DERIVATIVE
Without a non-linear activation between layers, stacking depth buys you nothing — the whole network collapses algebraically to a single linear layer. The activation function is what makes deep learning deep.

§ 01 — THE THRESHOLD CONCEPT

What this session exists to flip in your head

THE THRESHOLD CONCEPT

An activation function is the per-neuron Function<Double, Double> that runs after the weighted sum. The reason it exists isn’t to “do classification” — it’s to introduce non-linearity. Without a non-linear activation, no matter how many layers you stack, the network is mathematically equivalent to one linear layer. The choice of which activation to use is a menu, and the menu is split by where the activation sits (hidden vs. output) and what output range the layer needs.

Hold both halves of that sentence:

  • Why activations exist at all. Non-linearity preserves stacking depth. (Proof in §05, two lines.)
  • Why we choose between them. Range and gradient behaviour. Sigmoid outputs probabilities in (0, 1); tanh outputs in (−1, 1) and is zero-centred; ReLU outputs in [0, ∞) and never saturates on the positive side; the step function outputs {0, 1} and is not differentiable, which is why it can’t sit in a network we want to train by backprop.

The lecturer leads with the second half — “activations let the same framework do classification” — and underweights the first. We’ll lead with non-linearity, because that’s the half that makes the rest of the course make sense.

CHECK YOURSELFA 100-layer network with only ReLU activations between layers can model curves that no single linear layer can. A 100-layer network with no activations between layers (just stacked W·x + b operations) cannot. In your own words: why?
§ 02 — RECAP

The recap from Session 3 (don’t re-derive — link)

From Session 3, settled and carried forward:

  • The perceptron is a single artificial neuron: ŷ = m·x + b (one input feature) or ŷ = Σᵢ wᵢ·xᵢ + b (multiple features, one shared bias b — not one per feature, see Session 3 changelog row 7).
  • The loss is mean-squared error: J(m, b) = (1/N) · Σᵢ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ)².
  • The update rule (SGD, per-example, with the factor of 2 absorbed into η): m -= η · error · x, b -= η · error, where error = ŷ − y.
  • The stopping condition is gradient ≈ 0, not error = 0.

Today’s two additions: (i) a non-identity activation function gets wedged between the weighted sum and the output, and (ii) we derive the update rule from MSE rather than memorising it.

Carry-over correction. The lecturer re-states the Session 3 multi-feature form as y = m₁x₁ + b₁ + m₂x₂ + b₂ + m₃x₃ + b₃ = y again today. Same wrong form, same fix: there is one shared bias b, summed once at the end. Cross-reference Session3-Perceptron-GradientDescent-changelog.md row 7 for the full discussion.
§ 03 — THE PROBLEM

What activations solve

Concretely: a linear sum ŷ = Σ wᵢ·xᵢ + b is always a real number — possibly negative, possibly huge, possibly anything. That’s fine for predicting an AC price (a number); it’s useless if the answer you want is a class (“fraud” / “not fraud,” “rainy” / “windy” / “sunny,” “positive sentiment” / “negative sentiment”).

The fix the lecturer reaches for: pass ŷ through another function before reporting it. That post-processing function is the activation function. Different choices reshape the output range to whatever the downstream consumer needs:

  • For binary classification: a function whose range is (0, 1) so the output reads as a probability. → sigmoid.
  • For a use case where negative values are meaningful: a function whose range is (−1, 1). → tanh.
  • For a hidden layer that should keep positive signals and zero out negative ones (the modern default in deep networks): → ReLU.
  • For a hard binary {0, 1} decision with no probability: → step function, historically. (Why it fell out of fashion: §04a.)
  • For multi-class classification (3 or more classes): → softmax, which the lecturer doesn’t name. We’ll cover the gap in §06.
FAILURE TELLIf the layer’s outputs don’t match the task — sigmoid output on a regression problem, identity output on a classification problem, ReLU output on a regression problem that can produce negative numbers — training will either converge slowly, fail to converge, or converge to a model that silently misbehaves at inference. Match output activation to task first; everything else is decoration.
CHECK YOURSELFA model predicts daily temperature change in °C (can be negative). The architect wires ReLU as the output activation. What goes wrong, and what should they pick instead?
§ 04 — FOUR ACTIVATIONS

Formula, curve, range, role — for each of the four

Curves rendered by sampling the actual function at 400 points (not hand-drawn).

§04a — Step (Heaviside)

step(x) = { 1   if x ≥ 0
          { 0   if x < 0

Range: {0, 1}. Pure binary. This is the activation Rosenblatt’s 1958 perceptron used (Session 3 §03 — “the lecturer’s ‘perceptron’ today is not Rosenblatt’s — Rosenblatt’s uses this step”).

Why we don’t use it as a hidden-layer activation in modern networks. The lecturer calls the step function “outdated” without naming the underlying mechanism. The real reason: the step function is not differentiable at x = 0, and its derivative is exactly zero everywhere else. That breaks backpropagation, which depends on chain-rule-multiplied derivatives to propagate gradients through hidden layers (Session 5). A neuron whose activation has derivative zero contributes nothing to the gradient — the upstream weights get no update signal.

Where you still see it. As the output of a hard-decision binary classifier after the model has predicted a probability via sigmoid (you threshold the sigmoid at 0.5 to get a {0, 1} decision). The step is the thresholding step at inference time, not the activation that’s trained.

FAILURE TELLIf you ever wire a step function as a hidden-layer activation in a network you intend to train by backprop, the gradients for every layer below it will be exactly zero. The loss will not move. Symptom: “training is broken; no parameters are updating.” Cause: dead gradient through the step.

§04b — Sigmoid (σ)

σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e−x)

Range: (0, 1). Smooth, S-shaped, asymptotic at both ends. The closed-form derivative — a fact you’ll meet again in Session 5 — is elegant:

σ′(x) = σ(x) · (1 − σ(x))

That is: the derivative at any point is computable from the output of the sigmoid at that point. No re-evaluation needed.

What sigmoid is good for. Binary classification at the output. Train with binary-cross-entropy loss; the sigmoid output is the predicted probability of the positive class. Threshold at 0.5 (or any value, depending on cost asymmetry) to get a hard decision.

Correction — the most important in this session. The lecturer claims: “Sigmoid can be useful for multi-level classification, multi-category classification. For example, weather: rainy, windy, sunny — hard-code 0–0.3 = rainy, 0.31–0.6 = windy, 0.6+ = sunny.” This is wrong. Sigmoid outputs one number in (0, 1), interpretable as the probability of one class. For 3+ classes you need softmax (§06 below), which outputs a vector of K probabilities that sum to 1. The hard-coded threshold-band trick doesn’t work because:
  1. There’s nothing in the loss function to make the network put “rainy” examples in the (0, 0.3) band rather than the (0.6, 1) band. The network learned only that the right answer is some number; the band assignment is arbitrary.
  2. The decision boundaries fall on continuous slices of a 1D output rather than over discrete probability classes. A class assigned to (0, 0.3) is treated as one-third as “important” as one in (0.6, 1), but classes are nominal — they have no order.
  3. Adding a fourth class means re-shuffling all the bands; you can’t just add a new threshold.
Use softmax for multi-class. Production multi-class classifiers — every image classifier you’ve used, every text classifier, every language model’s next-token head — use softmax over the K classes.

Why sigmoid fell out of favour as a hidden-layer activation. Saturation. Far from x = 0, the sigmoid’s slope flattens to ~0 — meaning σ′(x) ≈ 0 for large |x|. During backprop, gradients get multiplied through every layer; when each multiplication is by ~0, the gradient vanishes before reaching the early layers. The early layers stop learning. This is the famous vanishing gradient problem (Hochreiter 1991; deeper treatment in Session 5).

FAILURE TELLIf you stack sigmoid activations through a deep network and find the early layers’ weights don’t change during training while the late layers do, you’ve hit vanishing gradients. The first fix is usually to swap sigmoid for ReLU in the hidden layers.

§04c — Hyperbolic tangent (tanh)

tanh(x) = (ex − e−x) / (ex + e−x)

Range: (−1, 1). Like a sigmoid that’s been recentred and stretched: tanh(x) = 2σ(2x) − 1. The closed-form derivative:

tanh′(x) = 1 − tanh²(x)

The real reason to choose tanh over sigmoid. The lecturer justifies tanh with a “charge / discharge current” example, but that’s about your input data, not the activation. The actual reason: tanh is zero-centred. Sigmoid outputs are always positive (in (0, 1)), which biases the gradients to the next layer’s weights to be one-signed — the optimiser then has to take a zigzag path through weight space. Tanh outputs sit symmetrically around 0, which gives cleaner gradient flow. Historically tanh was the hidden-layer default before ReLU.

Where tanh still lives in 2026. Inside LSTM and GRU gates (recurrent network cells from the 1997–2014 era — Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997, Cho et al. 2014). The “candidate cell state” in an LSTM is squashed by tanh; the gate values themselves are sigmoid. RNNs themselves have been largely displaced by Transformers (the topic next session), but tanh hasn’t disappeared — it just retreated into specific architectural roles.

Same vanishing-gradient problem as sigmoid. Tanh saturates at both extremes; deep stacks of tanh suffer the same vanishing gradient that sigmoid does. Same fix (ReLU).

§04d — ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)

ReLU(x) = max(0, x)

Range: [0, ∞). Piecewise linear. The derivative is:

ReLU′(x) = { 1   if x > 0
           { 0   if x < 0
           { undefined at x = 0  (by convention, 0)

Why ReLU is the modern hidden-layer default. Three reasons, all post-2012 (Krizhevsky et al. AlexNet popularised ReLU on ImageNet):

  1. No saturation on the positive side. A neuron whose pre-activation is +1000 still has gradient 1, not the ~0 you’d get from sigmoid or tanh. Gradients propagate.
  2. Cheap to compute and differentiate. max(0, x) is one comparison; the derivative is a constant 0 or 1. Compare with 1 / (1 + e−x) for sigmoid.
  3. Sparse activations. A randomly initialised ReLU network has roughly half its neurons output zero on any input. Sparsity helps generalisation.

Where the lecturer trips: “ReLU is for regression.” Half-truth. ReLU’s main role is as a hidden-layer activation in deep networks. For regression output:

  • Default: the identity (no activation). The output is W·hidden + b, which can be any real number. Train with MSE.
  • ReLU output is correct only when the target is known to be non-negative — counts, prices, durations, queue lengths. Wiring ReLU on a regression head whose targets can be negative (temperature deltas, returns, position offsets) clips every negative prediction to zero — silent under-prediction bias.
FAILURE TELL — “DYING RELU”A ReLU neuron whose pre-activation is negative for every training example will have derivative zero on every example, and its weights will never update. Once a neuron dies, it stays dead. Cause: usually a too-large learning rate that pushed the weights into the dead region. Fixes: lower the learning rate; switch to Leaky ReLU (max(0.01·x, x)) which has a small non-zero slope on the negative side; or use GELU / SiLU (smoother modern variants used in Transformers).

§ 05 — THE BIGGER REASON

Non-linearity preserves depth

This is the threshold concept made operational. Take a two-layer network with no activation between layers:

hidden  = W₁ · x   + b₁
output  = W₂ · hidden + b₂
        = W₂ · (W₁ · x + b₁) + b₂
        = (W₂ · W₁) · x + (W₂ · b₁ + b₂)
        = W′    · x + b′         ← a single linear layer

That’s two lines of high-school algebra. A stack of linear layers with no non-linearity in between is mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer. Add a hundred more layers — same conclusion. The expressive power of the model doesn’t grow; you just pay more compute for the same hypothesis class.

Now insert a non-linear activation between the layers:

hidden  = ReLU(W₁ · x + b₁)
output  = W₂ · hidden + b₂

The ReLU breaks the algebra. You can no longer fold W₁ and W₂ together into a single matrix; the composition is genuinely non-linear and can express things one linear layer can’t (curves, kinks, classification boundaries that aren’t hyperplanes). This is the entire reason we use activation functions in hidden layers. Without them, depth is decorative.

The universal approximation theorem (Cybenko 1989 for sigmoidal activations; Hornik 1991 generalised to bounded non-constant activations; sharpened by Leshno, Lin, Pinkus & Schocken 1993 to the necessary-and-sufficient condition “any non-polynomial activation”) makes this even sharper: a network with one hidden layer and enough neurons with any non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact set. In practice we stack many layers because depth gives the network a more parameter-efficient way to compose features — but the mathematical requirement for depth to matter at all is the activation function.

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

Two Function<double[], double[]> lambdas composed with no non-linearity in between are equivalent to a single matrix-multiply lambda — the JIT could collapse them automatically. With a non-linear function between them, the composition is genuinely a new function. The activation is what stops the optimiser (or the JIT) from eliminating your depth.

FAILURE TELLA “deep” network with no non-linear activations between layers will train no better than a single linear regression. Symptom: loss curve identical to the one-layer baseline. Cause: you’ve stacked depth that algebra silently folds away.
CHECK YOURSELFA colleague is debugging a “deep” model that performs identically to logistic regression. They’ve checked the learning rate, the optimiser, the data. What architectural mistake are they likely making?
§ 06 — HIDDEN vs. OUTPUT

The menu the lecturer never wrote

Two different jobs in a network, two different menus. The lecturer collapses them; making the distinction explicit fixes the sigmoid-for-multi-class mistake from §04b.

Hidden-layer activations (what runs between layers)

ACTIVATIONRANGEMODERN ROLEWHY
ReLU[0, ∞)Default for most hidden layersNo saturation on positive side; cheap; sparse
Leaky ReLU(−∞, ∞)When dying ReLU is observedSmall non-zero slope on negative side
GELU≈(−0.17, ∞)BERT, GPT-2/3/4, ViT FFN sub-layersSmoother than ReLU; small empirical wins
SwiGLU (gated SiLU variant)(−∞, ∞)LLaMA, PaLM, Mistral, Qwen FFN sub-layersModern frontier-LLM default; Shazeer 2020
tanh(−1, 1)LSTM/GRU candidate statesZero-centred; saturates → vanishing gradient
sigmoid(0, 1)LSTM/GRU gates onlySaturates; vanishing gradient in deep stacks
step{0, 1}Not used (non-differentiable)Breaks backprop

Output-layer activations (what’s on the final layer)

TASKOUTPUT ACTIVATIONLOSSWHAT THE OUTPUT MEANS
Regression (real-valued target)Identity (none)MSE (or MAE / Huber)The predicted value, in target units
Regression with non-negative targetReLU (or softplus)MSESame, clipped at 0
Binary classificationSigmoidBinary cross-entropyProbability of the positive class
Multi-class classification (mutually exclusive)SoftmaxCategorical cross-entropyVector of K probabilities summing to 1
Multi-label classification (each label independent)K sigmoids in parallelK binary cross-entropies summedProbability of each label, independently
SOFTMAX — THE FUNCTION THE LECTURER SHOULD HAVE INTRODUCED

Softmax generalises sigmoid to K classes. For a vector of K pre-activations z = (z₁, z₂, …, zK):

softmax(z)ᵢ  =  e(zi) / Σⱼ e(zj)

Each output is in (0, 1); they sum to 1; the largest pre-activation dominates the largest output (softmax is “soft” in that it doesn’t pick a winner outright, but the winner’s mass grows quickly with its lead). For the weather example — rainy / windy / sunny — the right architecture is: the final layer outputs 3 numbers (zrainy, zwindy, zsunny); softmax converts them to 3 probabilities that sum to 1; the predicted class is the one with the highest probability. Adding “cloudy” as a fourth class means adding one output unit and re-training. No threshold bands. No re-shuffling.

FAILURE TELLOutput activation and loss must be matched. Sigmoid + binary cross-entropy is one pairing; softmax + categorical cross-entropy is another; identity + MSE is the regression pairing. Mixing them (e.g. softmax + MSE, or sigmoid + categorical cross-entropy) produces gradients that don’t have the clean closed form you’d want, training is slow or unstable, and the resulting model is poorly calibrated.
CHECK YOURSELFYou’re building a classifier that says which one of {cat, dog, bird, fish} is in an image. What’s the output layer’s activation, and what loss do you train with?
§ 07 — THE MSE DERIVATIVE

The math the lecturer owed us from Session 3

Now to deliver Session 3’s promise. We want ∂J/∂m and ∂J/∂b from first principles for the linear model with MSE loss.

Setup. For one example (x, y) with prediction ŷ = m·x + b and per-example error error = ŷ − y:

J  =  (1/N) · Σᵢ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ)²
   =  (1/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ²

Step 1 — pull out the constant

∂J/∂m  =  (1/N) · Σᵢ ∂(errorᵢ²)/∂m

Step 2 — chain rule on errori²

Let u = errori. Then u² differentiates to 2u · (∂u/∂m):

∂(errorᵢ²)/∂m  =  2 · errorᵢ · (∂errorᵢ/∂m)

Step 3 — compute ∂errori/∂m

With errori = m·xi + b − yi, where m is the variable and xi, b, yi are all constants when we differentiate w.r.t. m:

∂errorᵢ/∂m  =  ∂(m·xᵢ + b − yᵢ)/∂m
              =  xᵢ + 0 − 0
              =  xᵢ

Step 4 — assemble

∂J/∂m  =  (1/N) · Σᵢ [2 · errorᵢ · xᵢ]
         =  (2/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ · xᵢ

Step 5 — same chain for b

∂(m·xi + b − yi)/∂b = 0 + 1 − 0 = 1, so:

∂J/∂b  =  (2/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ · 1
         =  (2/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ

Step 6 — fold the factor of 2 into the learning rate

The gradient-descent update is m_new = m_old − η · ∂J/∂m. The constant 2 multiplying ∂J/∂m is just a fixed scale; the user-chosen η is the adjustable scale. Absorb the 2:

ηeffective  =  η · 2  ← chosen by you anyway

m_new  =  m_old  −  ηeffective · (1/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ · xᵢ
b_new  =  b_old  −  ηeffective · (1/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ

For the per-example SGD update (one example at a time, drop the sum):

m_new  =  m_old  −  η · error · x
b_new  =  b_old  −  η · error

— exactly the form the lecturer asked us to memorise yesterday, now derived rather than asserted. The handout’s pages 12–13 carry the same derivation in the lecturer’s handwriting:

WHY THIS MATTERS OPERATIONALLY

The factor of 2 absorbing into η is the reason library implementations of MSE sometimes write the loss as (ŷ − y)² and sometimes as ½·(ŷ − y)². The half-factor cancels the 2 from the derivative, so the gradient becomes error · x exactly with no factor at all. Either convention is fine; just be consistent within a codebase. PyTorch’s nn.MSELoss uses (ŷ − y)² (no halving); some textbooks use ½·(ŷ − y)². The trained model is identical either way — only the printed loss values differ by a factor of 2.

CHECK YOURSELFRe-derive ∂J/∂b from scratch in your head, without looking. (If you can’t, the derivation hasn’t landed yet.)
§ 08 — THE CHAIN RULE

Named explicitly — because everything from here uses it

The move in §07 step 2 — “u² differentiates to 2u · (∂u/∂m)” — is the chain rule. The lecturer walks through it without naming it; let’s name it.

The chain rule. If y is a function of u, and u is a function of x, then:

dy/dx  =  (dy/du) · (du/dx)

In partial-derivative form, when y is a function of several intermediates each of which is a function of x:

∂y/∂x  =  Σᵢ (∂y/∂uᵢ) · (∂uᵢ/∂x)

The lecturer’s clean example: y = 2x, x = 2z. Then dy/dx = 2, dx/dz = 2, so dy/dz = 2 · 2 = 4. Directly verifiable: substituting, y = 2x = 2(2z) = 4z, so dy/dz = 4. ✓

Why the chain rule is the centre of gravity of deep learning. Every gradient in every neural network is a chain-rule product of per-layer derivatives. Backpropagation (Session 5) is the algorithm that computes those products efficiently, layer by layer, from the output back to the input. Today’s MSE derivation is the chain rule applied once: J = (error)², error = ŷ − y, ŷ = m·x + b. Three layers of substitution; three chain-rule multiplications. A deep network has dozens of layers; backprop is the chain rule applied dozens of times. Same rule. More layers.

NAMING NOTE

The chain rule is the calculus theorem. Backpropagation is the algorithm that applies the chain rule layer-by-layer through a neural network, with cached intermediate values so the same partial derivatives aren’t recomputed. They are not the same thing — the chain rule is the math, backprop is the engineering. (Same distinction lives in accuracy-traps.md row 4 of the skill; called out in Session 3 §09 as well.)

CHECK YOURSELFIn one sentence, what’s the difference between the chain rule and backpropagation?
§ 09 — FORWARD + BACKWARD

What “one step” of training actually does

Now we can name the two-phase loop the training algorithm runs at every step:

  1. Feedforward pass. Start with the input x. Apply each layer’s W · h + b (then activation), in order, from input to output. The final layer produces ŷ. Compute the loss J(ŷ, y).
  2. Backpropagation pass. Start from the loss. Use the chain rule to compute ∂J/∂W and ∂J/∂b for every W and b in the network — from the output layer back to the input layer. Update each parameter via the gradient-descent rule: param -= η · ∂J/∂param.

For our single-perceptron model (Session 3 + this one), the feedforward pass is ŷ = m·x + b; the backprop pass is the §07 derivation; the update is m -= η·error·x; b -= η·error. One feedforward + one backprop = one training step (one iteration). Repeat across every example in the training set; that’s one epoch.

FAILURE TELLIf your loss starts at a sensible value, drops a bit on the first step, then stops moving entirely — you have a wiring bug in the backprop pass, not (as one might guess) a dead ReLU. Likeliest culprits: the optimiser isn’t actually stepping (.step() not called in PyTorch); gradients aren’t accumulating (.zero_grad() not called between steps); or the loss isn’t connected to the labels in the right way. First diagnostic: print a parameter before and after .step() and check it changed.
CHECK YOURSELFIn one sentence each: what does the feedforward pass compute, and what does the backprop pass compute?
§ 10 — EPOCH · ITERATION · BATCH

Three definitions and the arithmetic that ties them together

  • Iteration (or step). One forward pass + one backward pass + one parameter update. The atomic unit of training.
  • Batch / mini-batch. A subset of the training data used in one iteration. Choose:
    • Full batch (whole dataset per step) — clean but slow per step; you only update once per epoch.
    • Mini-batch (typically 32–512 examples per step) — the production default; balances noise and throughput.
    • Single example (batch size = 1) — pure SGD; very noisy, very fast per step.
  • Batch size. How many examples are in one batch. Not to be confused with batch number (how many batches make up one epoch).
  • Epoch. One full pass through the entire training dataset. If the dataset has N examples and the batch size is B, then one epoch = N / B iterations.

Worked example (the lecturer’s). Dataset: 2,000 rows. Batch size: 500. Then:

batches per epoch  =  2,000 / 500  =  4 iterations

If we train for 30 epochs: 30 × 4 = 120 total iterations (parameter updates).

WHY BATCH SIZE IS A KNOB

Smaller batches → noisier gradient estimates but more updates per epoch (often helps generalisation; sometimes helps escape saddle points). Larger batches → smoother gradient estimates but fewer updates per epoch (better for GPU throughput; tends to need a larger learning rate to compensate). The trade-off has its own large literature (Smith et al. 2018 Don’t Decay the Learning Rate, Increase the Batch Size); for today, internalise that batch size and learning rate are coupled, and treat the defaults (batch_size ≈ 32–256, lr ≈ 1e-3 to 1e-4 for Adam) as starting points to tune.

FAILURE TELL — VANISHING MEMORYIf you crank batch size up too far for your GPU, you get out-of-memory errors. The fix isn’t always “buy a bigger GPU” — it’s often gradient accumulation: run several small batches sequentially, accumulate the gradients, then step the optimiser once. The effect is identical to a large batch, with smaller peak memory.
CHECK YOURSELFDataset has 60,000 examples. Batch size is 64. How many iterations per epoch? (Answer: 60,000 / 64 = 937.5, so 938 if the final partial batch is kept — the PyTorch DataLoader default with drop_last=False; or 937 if the partial batch is dropped.)

  • Softmax + categorical cross-entropy. The output activation + loss pairing that the §06 correction promised.
  • Backpropagation through multiple layers. The §08 chain-rule machinery applied to a real multi-layer network, with the matrix-form derivatives. Vanishing and exploding gradients (and their fixes — gradient clipping, careful initialisation, BatchNorm / LayerNorm, skip connections).
  • A worked multi-layer example. Forward and backward passes on a 2-layer network with ReLU hidden activation and sigmoid output, end-to-end.
  • The training-loop knobs the lecturer named today — epoch, batch size, learning rate — in the context of a real code example. Her promised sentiment-analysis project (3 lakh Amazon comments, Keras) is where these stop being abstract.

The handout pages 14–22 cover most of this (batch / mini-batch / stochastic GD trade-offs, momentum-based GD with the vt = γ·vt−1 + η∇wt rule). I’ll fold those into the next session’s notes when they’re taught.

CHECK YOURSELFWithout re-reading: name the four activation functions covered today, give each one’s output range, and say which is the only sensible default for a hidden layer in a deep network in 2026.
§ 12 — DIAGNOSTIC TABLE

Symptom → cause → fix

SYMPTOMLIKELY CAUSEFIX
“Deep” network performs identically to a linear baselineNo non-linear activation between layers; the depth is folding away algebraicallyInsert ReLU (or any non-linear activation) between the linear layers
Multi-class classifier with a single sigmoid output; some classes never predictedHard-coded threshold bands don’t have a loss signal that puts each class in its band; the network has no incentive to use the bandsSwitch to softmax output + categorical cross-entropy; one output per class
Regression model on a target that can be negative; predictions clipped at 0ReLU on the output layerSwitch output activation to identity (or use Leaky ReLU / linear)
Training “doesn’t move” — loss flat from epoch 1Step (or other non-differentiable) activation in a hidden layer; or wiring bug in the backprop pass(i) Replace step with a differentiable activation. (ii) Diagnose backprop: print a parameter before and after .step()
Early layers’ weights don’t change; late layers’ weights doVanishing gradients from saturating activations (sigmoid / tanh) stacked deepSwap sigmoid / tanh hidden activations for ReLU; consider gradient clipping; consider better initialisation (Xavier / He)
Some ReLU neurons “stop firing” — pre-activation negative for all examplesDying ReLU; learning rate too large pushed weights into the dead regionReduce learning rate; switch to Leaky ReLU; consider GELU / SiLU
Output activation and loss don’t match (e.g. softmax + MSE)Mismatched pairing; gradients are messyMatch: sigmoid + BCE, softmax + CCE, identity + MSE
Out-of-memory error when training with a large batchGPU can’t hold the activations + gradients of that batchReduce batch size; use gradient accumulation; mixed-precision training
§ 13 — QUIZ YOURSELF

Ten questions

Recall

  1. State the four activation functions covered in this session and their output ranges.
  2. What is the derivative of the sigmoid function, in terms of σ(x) itself?
  3. Why is the step function not used as a hidden-layer activation in modern networks?

Application

  1. You’re building a sentiment classifier with 5 categories: very negative / negative / neutral / positive / very positive. What output activation, and what loss?
  2. You’re predicting house prices (always positive). The architect wires identity as the output activation. Does this work, and if so, when does it not?
  3. Re-derive ∂J/∂b from J = (1/N) · Σᵢ (m·xᵢ + b − yᵢ)², showing every step.
  4. A network with 3 hidden layers and tanh activations everywhere is showing very slow training on its earlier layers. Diagnose, and propose two fixes.

Debugging

  1. A “deep” network with 10 hidden layers and no activations between them performs identically to a single linear regression on the same data. Why?
  2. A multi-class classifier built with a single sigmoid output + 4 hard-coded threshold bands gives 40% accuracy on a balanced 4-class problem. What’s structurally wrong with the architecture?
  3. Plain-English chain. For a single training example (x = 30, y = 35) with current (m = 1, b = 5, η = 0.01): what did we predict? How wrong were we? What does each of m and b change to in the next step? Why doesn’t anything change here in particular?
ANSWERS
  1. Step: {0, 1}. Sigmoid: (0, 1). Tanh: (−1, 1). ReLU: [0, ∞).
  2. σ′(x) = σ(x) · (1 − σ(x)). Computable directly from the activation’s output.
  3. Non-differentiable at x = 0 and derivative = 0 elsewhere → breaks backpropagation. Gradients can’t propagate through a step.
  4. Softmax output with 5 units, trained with categorical cross-entropy. The output is a 5-vector of probabilities summing to 1; the predicted class is the argmax.
  5. Identity works for regression because prices are real-valued. It works here in particular because prices happen to be positive — but identity doesn’t enforce positivity. If you wanted hard guarantees that ŷ ≥ 0, you’d use ReLU or softplus on the output. Most regression heads in practice use identity and accept occasional negative predictions during training.
  6. ∂J/∂b = (1/N) · Σᵢ ∂(errorᵢ²)/∂b = (1/N) · Σᵢ 2·errorᵢ·(∂errorᵢ/∂b) = (1/N) · Σᵢ 2·errorᵢ·1 = (2/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ. The 2 folds into η as before.
  7. Vanishing gradient through stacked tanh — tanh saturates at both extremes, gradients are ~0 there, and the chain-rule product to the early layers collapses to ~0. Fixes: (i) swap hidden activations to ReLU; (ii) careful initialisation (Xavier/He) plus gradient clipping; (iii) skip connections (Session 5+).
  8. No non-linearity between layers means the stack collapses algebraically: W₃(W₂(W₁ x + b₁) + b₂) + b₃ = W′ x + b′. One linear layer wearing ten layers’ makeup. The fix is to insert ReLU between the linear layers.
  9. Sigmoid outputs one scalar in (0, 1); there’s no loss signal that puts each class in its band — the network learns one number, the band assignment is arbitrary. Switch to softmax + categorical cross-entropy with 4 output units.
  10. Predict: ŷ = 1·30 + 5 = 35. Error: 35 − 35 = 0. m and b: unchanged. Why nothing moves: the prediction is exactly right on this example, so the per-example loss is zero, so the per-example gradient is zero, so the update is zero. The other examples in the batch / epoch will move the parameters; this one is a no-op.

§ 14 — GLOSSARY

The vocabulary of this session

Activation function
A Function<Double, Double> (or Function<Vector, Vector>) applied after a neuron’s weighted sum. Today’s four: step, sigmoid, tanh, ReLU. Plus softmax (multi-class output) and friends (GELU, SiLU, Leaky ReLU).
Backpropagation pass
The phase of one training step that computes gradients of the loss w.r.t. every parameter, by applying the chain rule layer by layer from output back to input.
Batch / mini-batch
A subset of the training dataset processed in one iteration. Choose the size to balance gradient noise, update frequency, and GPU memory.
Batch size
The number of examples in one batch. Common values: 32, 64, 128, 256. Coupled to the learning rate (larger batch typically wants larger lr).
Chain rule
The calculus theorem dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx) (single-variable) or ∂y/∂x = Σ (∂y/∂uᵢ)·(∂uᵢ/∂x) (multi-variable). The mechanism backpropagation applies layer by layer.
Dying ReLU
A failure mode where a ReLU neuron’s pre-activation goes negative for all training examples; gradient becomes 0; the neuron’s weights never update. Fixes: lower lr, Leaky ReLU, GELU/SiLU.
Epoch
One full pass through the entire training dataset. If the dataset has N examples and batch size is B, one epoch = N/B iterations.
Feedforward pass
The phase of one training step that runs input → output through every layer to compute the prediction and the loss.
Hidden-layer activation
The activation applied to a neuron’s output inside the network (not the final layer). Modern default: ReLU.
Hyperbolic tangent (tanh)
(ex−e−x)/(ex+e−x). Range (−1, 1). Zero-centred. Saturates → vanishing gradient when stacked deep.
Iteration / step
One feedforward + one backpropagation + one parameter update. The atomic unit of training.
Non-linearity
The property of a function that’s not of the form a·x + b. The reason activation functions exist: without one, stacking layers collapses to a single linear layer.
Output-layer activation
The activation on the final layer of a network. Choose by task: identity for regression, sigmoid for binary classification, softmax for multi-class.
ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)
max(0, x). Range [0, ∞). The modern default hidden-layer activation. Cheap, non-saturating on positive side, can “die” on the negative side.
Saturation
When an activation’s output is at the flat end of its range and its derivative is ~0. Sigmoid and tanh saturate at both extremes; ReLU saturates on the negative side only.
Sigmoid (σ)
1/(1+e−x). Range (0, 1). Output reads as a probability. Derivative is σ(x)·(1−σ(x)). Output activation for binary classification. Vanishing gradient when used as a hidden activation.
Softmax
softmax(z)ᵢ = e(zi) / Σⱼ e(zj). Generalises sigmoid to K classes. Output is a probability vector summing to 1. The output activation for multi-class classification (the function the lecturer should have introduced).
Step / threshold / Heaviside
1 if x ≥ 0 else 0. Range {0, 1}. The activation in Rosenblatt’s 1958 perceptron. Not differentiable → can’t backprop → not used as a hidden activation today.
Vanishing gradient
A failure mode in deep networks where gradients shrink to ~0 as they propagate back through layers, because each layer’s local derivative is small. Stacked sigmoids and tanh’s are the classic cause. Fix: ReLU, or careful initialisation, or skip connections.
